title: Verses as signs
hook: each verse is an ayah, a sign, like the signs in nature

segments.voice: Yesterday, surah: one hundred and fourteen of them. Your line: longest to shortest.

A road sign isn't the city. It points to the city: you see it and know something is out there, ahead of you. Now a sunset. The way your breath keeps going while you sleep. Two strangers who become family. Rain on dry ground. The Qur'an has one word for all of these, and it's the very same word it uses for its own verses.
screen: `A ROAD SIGN ISN'T THE CITY.` → `A SUNSET, A BREATH, THE RAIN.` → `ONE WORD FOR ALL OF THEM.`

segments.voice: Each verse of the Qur'an is called an ayah. The word means a sign, a token, a mark that points past itself. In everyday Arabic, an ayah could be a signal, a landmark, a wonder. The Qur'an uses it for three kinds of things, and doesn't fence them apart. The verses on the page are ayat. The miracles of the prophets are ayat: Musa's staff, the she-camel of Salih. And the world is full of ayat. In Pickthall's words: "Lo! In the creation of the heavens and the earth and (in) the difference of night and day are tokens (of His sovereignty) for men of understanding." Pickthall says tokens there, but the Arabic is the same word as verses. Surah 30 lists signs one after another, the heavens and the earth, "and the difference of your languages and colours." And another verse, in Pickthall: "We shall show them Our portents on the horizons and within themselves." Portents, tokens, signs: all ayat. So when a Muslim reads a verse, or watches rain come down on dry ground, the Qur'an asks for the same kind of attention: not only what is this, but what does it point to? How many ayat are there? It depends whom you ask. The early schools of reciters placed a few verse breaks differently, so printed copies don't all give the same total. The words are the same; only where one verse ends and the next begins differs. And that's the heart of it. A verse isn't only a sentence to understand. It's a sign to follow, like everything else the Qur'an calls a sign.
screen: `AYAH: A SIGN THAT POINTS PAST ITSELF` · `VERSES, MIRACLES AND THE WORLD` · `ON THE HORIZONS AND WITHIN` · `A VERSE IS FOLLOWED, NOT ONLY READ`

segments.voice: Go to a window or step out the door if you can; if not, close your eyes and listen. Let your attention land on one ordinary thing, a tree, the light on a wall, a bird, the hum of traffic, your own pulse, and without analyzing it, look at it the way you'd look at a road sign and ask quietly: what does this point to? Let the question stay open.
Ayah. A verse of the Qur'an, and a sign: in one word, the page and the world. Today's word.
Your line: a verse is a sign. On the page, and in the world. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims call each verse of the Qur'an an ayah, a sign, and the Qur'an asks its readers to reflect on the signs in creation as well as on the verses of the book.

fork.setup: you're watching rain fall on dry ground. what does the Qur'an ask you to do with it?
options: ignore it, since it isn't scripture.
read it like a verse: ask what it points to.
fork.reveal: the Qur'an calls the rain, the night and day, even your own languages, ayat: the same word as its verses.

original.note: Arabic: a sign, a token, a wonder, and a verse of the Qur'an. plural: ayat.

what it means: a sign that points past itself, in the text and in the world.
what a scholar hears: one word for verse, miracle and natural sign, and verse totals that vary between the early schools only in where the breaks fall.
